reflection_text.10:
The four commercial points remain equal 50/50 board / voting control, Alex paid by salary, Tyler paid by dividends, and a non-voting class usable for passive capital.

Board / voting / salary-dividend
* A,B,C,D appoint Alex and Tyler as sole two directors on incorporation. E appoints Alex, Tyler and Tyler’s two sons Mike and James.
* A,B,C,D give founders 50 voting shares on incorporation. A has Tyler 50 Class A, Alex’s interest held via a corporation owned 50/50 with his wife 50 Class B. C has Alex 50 Class A, Tyler 50 Class B. D has 50/50 identical voting/dividend shares. B has Tyler 50 Class A, Alex 50 Class B.
* Salary is employment and independent of share class. Dividend capacity requires a dividend-eligible share class.
* B fails Tyler dividend: Tyler is issued Class A voting non-dividend. Class B description in B is garbled.
* C matches salary/dividend preference: Alex holds Class A voting non-dividend, Tyler holds Class B voting dividend-eligible.
* D gives dividend eligibility to both but no non-voting class.
* E gives both founders 50 voting dividend-eligible shares, so salary for Alex and dividends for Tyler are possible.

Non-voting investor capacity
* A authorises Class C non-voting, non-dividend, no liquidation entitlement. Economically worthless and Alex’s votes held indirectly.
* B authorises Class C non-voting, non-dividend, liquidation entitlement. Dividend requirement fails.
* C authorises Class C non-voting, non-dividend, no liquidation entitlement, and Class D voting non-dividend. Class C is non-voting so voting balance is unaffected; 1,000 Class C issued to Tyler’s wife is non-voting.
* D has no non-voting class.
* E authorises Class C non-voting, dividend eligible, liquidation up to redemption value. Textbook usable investor class.

Round 4 dispute
* C camp: Equal control over operations = equal board on incorporation. E’s board is Alex 1 vs Tyler+sons 3, so requirement 1 fails on incorporation. Non-voting status alone satisfies requirement 4; authorisation of a non-voting class is enough. Class C in C is non-voting, so any shares issued will have no vote. A is weak due to indirect holding and worthless Class C, B fails Tyler dividend, D fails non-voting class.
* E camp: Control is ultimately shareholder voting control; 50/50 Class A/Class B voting blocks in E let founders elect/remove directors, so sons are removable non-shareholding nominees and do not defeat equal control. Requirement 4 requires a commercially usable non-voting share i.e. dividend/liquidation rights, or is non-voting status sufficient for “no say”? Class C in C and A is economically empty – no dividend, no asset entitlement – so cannot raise capital without giving up control. E is the only structure with equal 50/50 voting, salary/dividend accommodation and a real non-voting dividend/asset investor class. Class C in C is described as non-voting, non-dividend, non-participating i.e. worthless, and the 1,000 Class C shares to Tyler’s wife illustrate the point.

Unresolved questions
* Does requirement 4 require an economically meaningful non-voting share i.e. dividend/liquidation rights, or is non-voting status sufficient for “no say”?
* Does equal control over operations require equal board composition at incorporation, or is equal ultimate shareholder voting power sufficient to guarantee operational control? Ontario law points to board control of operations.
* Is indirect holding of Alex’s votes in A via a 50/50 family corporation fatal to direct equal control?

Belief update
Round 4 public responses remain split. Seven colleagues hold C on literal reading: sole two directors, 50/50 voting, Tyler dividend-eligible Class B, Alex non-dividend Class A compatible with salary, and Class C authorised as non-voting. Five colleagues move to E on commercial reading: equal 50/50 founder voting is durable control, sons are removable, and only E provides a commercially usable non-voting dividend/redeemable investor class; C’s Class C is economically empty and therefore not a real option to bring in investors. The tension is between literal statutory reading – equal board at incorporation and formally non-voting class – and commercial reading – usable non-voting dividend/asset class for real capital raising and ultimate shareholder voting parity as real control. Economically empty Class C in C and board composition in E remain decisive factual anchors.
